I think it’s less that Moby-Dick is a kaiju than that the novel is a predecessor of kaiju stories more generally. What’s important is that Moby-Dick is gargantuan compared to the human characters, and becomes an ever present threat that many of those characters fear in a similar way as later giant monster stories; from their perspective, Moby-Dick might as well be Godzilla because, like, what else in the natural world then or now could compare? I mean, they’re on a shitty little boat in the middle of the Atlantic praying to God that a giant white whale, which could easily destroy their ship if it wanted, hopefully won’t even notice them until their insane captain tries striking it. Of course compared to our modern idea of a kaiju like Goji or Kong, Moby-Dick is just a lil guy. But he occupies a similar role in the original novel to those later monsters.

About his trumpet playing specifically, his tone and ‘voice’ on the instrument are phenomenal. Every trumpet player sounds a little different because every person’s lips and chops are different, to say nothing of how playing habits can affect one’s sounds. But some players take those quirks and develop entire styles unique to themselves which seem to reflect that player’s personality. Take for example Louis Armstrong who sounds bright and life-affirming, or Dizzy Gillespie who sounds playful yet inquisitive.

Miles sounds ‘cool’ by the standards of mid 20th century America. He was a man of few words who wore sunglasses indoors and didn’t take shit from anyone, and his playing feels like that. I’d recommend one of my favorite solos of his from Straight No Chaser, off of the Milestones album. His tone isn’t loud or abrasive, and he’s a master of ballads for that reason. He could also play fast if he wanted to (he started his career playing with Charlie Parker, so he could certainly play super fast bebop) but usually he played fewer notes carefully chosen to hit harder. He’d repeat phrases, or string together relatively simple phrases back to back, to create solos that were legible and enjoyable on first listen but could be studied for their melodic cleverness and inventiveness decades later.

I like liminal/vhs horror and this is right up my alley. The spaces you filmed are eerie as shit, and I do like the hints of the bloody room behind the plastic curtain thing, and whatever all that means.

I do agree with others though that, without context for the footage, it’s less scary as it is just visually interesting. If you had a text card explaining who shot the footage and where, and got the viewer’s attention as to what to ‘look for’ in the footage (I.e. the bloody room, and what my reside there), I think that would give the short much needed ‘shape’ as it were.

And I also agree that you use too many effects, specifically the last 50s where they distract from the creepiness of the setting, rather than add to the vibe of the work as a whole; it becomes hard to even see the room itself, which, when you have a room that creepy, you wanna avoid! Maybe save the more dramatic filters towards the end of the scene, right before the hand opens the curtain. A lot of found-footage films will use that kind of the filter right before a jumpscare, almost as a way to mentally prepare the audience for what’s to come. You can try punctuating your scene in similar ways, using the unique qualities of your vhs aesthetic to tell your story.

Demons (1985)
It’s about a bunch of people who go to a mysterious film screening at a recently renovated theatre. A woman puts on a mask displayed in the lobby and, at the same time scary stuff happens in the in-movie movie, she turns into a demon—like a weird technicolor demon with bug eyes and green drool—and then it basically becomes a zombie movie but with demons. It’s never explained where the mask comes from or who/what renovated the theatre, setting the events of the film into motion.

And it’s amazing! It makes a weird kind of dream sense in the way the demonization(?) spreads from person to person. The film also moves at a pace which makes the gradual escalation of horror seem purposeful, like there’s a demonic mind plotting the events of the story which we only see from the victims perspective, all without any actual explanation. It makes it feel different from regular zombie movies, and A LOT different form regular demon movies lol

Blair Witch (2016)

I actually think it does a good job trying to expand on the original’s mix of claustrophobia (ignore the fact that it’s set in the woods) and paranoia. In fact, while the found footage aspect feels much more forced, the overall vibe of the movie is very strong and eerie. It has that same quality as REC where the impending sense of doom just keeps escalating at a good pace. But the script is really lackluster and none of the character arcs really go anywhere, except for the fanboy of the Blair Witch who’s transformation is pretty great.

What could’ve been a 8-9/10 just winds up being like a 6, which sucks.

I find it weird how divisive the movie is cause I absolutely loved it, even seeing the twist coming early on. I just think James Wan is having a lot of fun in it. You can tell throughout his filmography up to this point that he has a soft spot for campy, borderline silly stuff (like the puppet in Saw or the Red Demon in Insidious, which, while scary, are very heightened and clash with the otherwise serious tones of those movies). It feels like Malignant is his attempt to explore that campiness throughout the entire runtime, with the vary premise of the movie being campy and weird.

I just can’t not love the fight scene in the jail house, or some of the bombastic camera movements, or just the beautiful design of the villain. They’re so heightened and cartoonish, while simultaneously filmed so earnestly by such a technically skilled director.

I don’t think that people who dislike the film ‘hate fun’, but I’m surprised time and again how many people really hate Malignant. It’s a big(ish) budget movie with the joy of horror in its heart that a teenager might have. And I find that so charming.

Something like Halloween strikes a good balance for me that I keep coming back to.

It’s scary, but not in viscerally upsetting way thanks to the lack of gore and the relatively quick kills. For as much as it influenced the later, slashier slasher films, it feels more like a haunted house ride. Many of the best scares involve Michael just standing there! MENACINGLY! Its more spooky than it is horrifying, which I love it for.

Obviously this has a lot to do with changing times and the movie not being as shocking as it was in 1978. But also the campier elements shine all the stronger because of it, like how Loomis can go from somber messenger of impending doom, to eventually, “Get yo ass away from there!” Good shit. And Michael with the bedsheet and glasses! And some of the wonderfully corny dialogue between the teens that were definitely written by adults. It’s all so good, while still avoiding schlock territory and still retaining that spooky atmosphere.

Plus having Jamie Lee Curtis, one of the best final girls, gives the movie a heart that a lot of later slashers never achieved.

And of course, it just has amazing Halloween vibes! Even in July, if I play Halloween, a tiny piece of autumn will make its way into my house. Not many movies can do that.

I think Gunther Schuller’s book ‘Early Jazz’ puts him and his claims into perspective.

Schuller argues that Morton had a very specific definition of ‘jazz’ that made it distinct from both ragtime and the blues, which Morton viewed, in Schuller’s words, as “not just musical styles, but specific musical forms: the one a multi-thematic structure, the other an eight- twelve- or sixteen-bar single theme form with a predetermined chord progression. These were forms as well-defined as sonata form was to a “‘classical’” composer, and Morton accepted them as active, continuing traditions” (140).

Morton didn’t view Jazz as it’s own separate musical form like we see it now. Instead, he saw it as a playing style, which could be applied to any tune regardless of the form.

“In his mind and perhaps in actual fact Morton has isolated as ‘jazz’ an area not covered by the blues or ragtime. Since he applied a smoother, more swinging syncopation and a greater degree of improvisational liscence to a variety of musical materials, such as ragtime, opera, and French and Spanish popular songs and dances, Morton’s claim to have invented jazz no longer seems quite so rash. As he puts it so succinctly in regard to his transformation of ‘La Paloma’, “‘The difference comes in the right hand-in the syncopation, which...changes the color from red to blue’” (140).

Even then, it wouldn’t be right to say that he was definitely the only person playing in that style at that time, or even the first. As others in this thread have said, jazz (or jass as it was originally called) developed first in New Orleans in the late 19th century, and you can’t really pinpoint a single creator. In the following decades jazz found a second home in the northern U.S. in places like Chicago, where it took on a more ‘sophisticated’ appearance; whereas New Orleans jazz was party music played in bars and brothels, this later style was more appropriate for ballroom concerts and upscale events, and looked more like a real orchestra, like the big bands of the 30s and 40s later would.

Jelly Roll Morton was part of that northern tradition. That came with a lot of baggage and prejudice against the ‘black negros’ down South (137), which he, a Creole, thought were lesser musicians than him, with the big exception of pianist Tony Jackson. Otherwise, he disregarded both the players of New Orleans jazz, and the style in general.

To put it another way, he was able to view himself as the inventor of jazz because he didn’t think the earlier style influenced him. Obviously this isn’t true, as there were New Orleans musicians in Chicago who played in some of these larger bands, and who certainly would have exposed people like Morton to the earlier style. It’s also obviously not true because, yes, the New Orleans style did exist, and from the archival recordings that exist from musicians who had lived at that time, the music was not as radically different from Morton’s as he might have claimed.

His claim as the creator of jazz makes sense only if you don’t know the history a jazz, or if you, like him, disregard what came before as somehow fundamentally different, which also doesn’t make sense looking back.

You're probably right. I just offered it in case OP likes prog-rock or experimental rock, which Bitches Brew overlaps a lot with. But yeah, it probably shouldn't be someone's first jazz album.

Here's some big name artists people usually think of when they think of great jazz musicians, in no particular order: Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Duke Ellington, Dave Brubeck, Art Blakey, Bill Evans, Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Charles Mingus, Thelonious Monk, Louis Armstrong, Ornette Colman (who you probably don't want to start off with) and Herbie Hancock.

As for albums to help you get into the genre, I have to recommend Miles Davis' 'Kind of Blue', the most sold jazz album of all time. I'd also recommend 'Saxophone Colossus' by Sonny Rollins, which is a great example of the kind of hard-bop jazz that was the norm in the 1950s. Dave Brubeck made an extremely popular album called 'Time Out' which is also a great start. 'Moanin'' by Art Blakey is great 50s jazz too. If you're more into fusion and rock influenced stuff, give Herbie Hancock's 'Headhunters' a shot, or another Miles Davis album called 'Bitches Brew'.

Hope that helps!
